# AF 第二章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 2

[P01] Three nights later old Major died in his sleep. He was buried at the foot of the orchard in early March. This was early in March. During the three months, there was much secret activity. Major's speech had given the clever animals a new way of looking at life. They did not know when the uprising（起义） would happen. They had no reason to think it would be in their lifetime, but they saw it was their duty to get ready. The pigs, seen as the cleverest animals, did the work of teaching and organising the others.

[P02] The most important pigs were two young boars（公猪）, Snowball and Napoleon. Mr. Jones was raising them to sell. Napoleon was big and fierce-looking. He was the only Berkshire（伯克郡） boar（公猪） on the farm. He did not talk much, but he always got his own way. Snowball was livelier, spoke faster and had more new ideas, but people did not think he had the same depth of character. The other male（雄性） pigs were fat porkers（肉猪）. The best known was a small fat pig named Squealer. He had round cheeks, twinkling（闪烁） eyes, quick movements, and a high, sharp（锋利） voice. He was a brilliant（聪明的） talker. When he argued a difficult point, he would skip（跳跃） from side to side and whisk（搅拌） his tail, and somehow（不知怎的） this was very persuasive（有说服力）.

[P03] The others said of Squealer that he could turn black into white. These three pigs had worked old Major's teachings（教导） into a full system of thought, and they gave it the name Animalism（动物主义）. Several nights a week, after Mr. Jones was asleep, they held secret meetings in the barn（谷仓） and explained the principles（原则） of Animalism（动物主义） to the others.

[P04] At first, many animals were stupid and did not care. Some said they must be loyal（忠诚） to Mr. Jones and called him "Master." They said, "Mr. Jones feeds us. If he were gone, we should starve（饿死） to death." Others asked, "Why should we care what happens after we are dead?" or "If this uprising is to happen anyway, what difference does it make whether we work for it or not?", which the pigs said was against the spirit of Animalism. The pigs had trouble making them see this was against the spirit of Animalism. The stupidest questions came from Mollie, the white mare（母马）.

[P05] The first thing she asked Snowball was: "Will there still be sugar after the uprising?" "No," said Snowball firmly. "We cannot make sugar on this farm. Besides, you do not need sugar. You will have all the oats（燕麦） and hay（干草） you want." "And can I still wear ribbons（丝带） in my mane（鬃毛）?" "Comrade," asked Mollie."Comrade（同志）," said Snowball, "those ribbons you love so much are the badge（标志） of slavery（奴役）. Can you not see that liberty（自由） is worth more than ribbons?" Mollie agreed, but she did not sound sure. The pigs had an even harder time fighting the lies of Moses, the tame（驯服） raven（乌鸦）.

[P06] Moses was Mr. Jones's special pet. He was a spy（间谍） and told tales, but also a clever talker. He said he knew a mysterious country called Sugarcandy（糖块） Mountain. All animals went there when they died, up in the sky, a little beyond the clouds. There it was Sunday seven days a week. Clover was in season all year round, and lump（块） sugar and linseed（亚麻籽） cake grew on the hedges（树篱）. The animals hated Moses because he told tales and did no work. But some believed in Sugarcandy（糖块） Mountain. The pigs had to talk hard to persuade them that there was no such place. Their most faithful（忠诚） followers（追随者） were Boxer and Clover.

[P07] These two found it hard to think for themselves. But once they accepted the pigs as teachers, they took in everything and passed it to the others in simple words. They never missed the secret meetings in the barn and led the singing of 'Beasts（野兽） of England', which ended every meeting. Disciple（门徒） Now the uprising came much earlier than anyone had expected. In past years Mr. Jones was a hard master, but a capable（有能力） farmer. Later he had bad days. He lost money in a lawsuit（诉讼）, became very sad, and began to drink too much.

[P08] For days he sat in his Windsor（温莎） chair in the kitchen, reading newspapers, drinking, and sometimes feeding Moses bread soaked（湿透） in beer. His men were idle（无所事事的） and dishonest（不诚实）. The fields were full of weeds（杂草）. The buildings needed new roofs. The hedges were not cared for, and the animals were hungry. June came and the hay was almost ready. On Midsummer（仲夏）'s Eve（前夕）, a Saturday, Mr. Jones went to Willingdon. On Midsummer's Eve, which was a Saturday, Mr. Jones went into Willingdon and got so drunk at the Red Lion that he did not come back until midday on Sunday.

[P09] The men milked the cows early, then went hunting rabbits. They gave the animals no food. When Mr. Jones came home, he fell asleep at once on the sofa, with the News of the World over his face. So by evening the animals still had nothing to eat. At last they could bear it no longer. One cow broke the store-shed door with her horn, and all the animals began to eat from the bins. Just then Mr. Jones woke up. The next moment he and his four men were in the store-shed with whips, hitting out in all directions.

[P10] This was too much for the hungry animals. They all rushed at their tormentors（折磨者） together, though they had planned nothing before. Jones and his men suddenly found animals butting and kicking them from every side. They could not control the situation at all. They had never seen animals act like this before. The sudden uprising of creatures（生物） they were used to beating and treating badly as they liked frightened them almost out of their wits（智慧）. After a moment or two they stopped trying to defend（保卫） themselves and ran away. A minute later all five of them were running fast down the cart-track to the main road, with the animals chasing（追赶） them in triumph（胜利）.

[P11] Jones looked out of the bedroom window, saw what was happening, quickly threw a few things into a carpet（地毯） bag, and slipped（滑倒） out by another way. Moses jumped off his perch and flapped（拍打） after her, croaking（呱呱叫） loudly. Meanwhile（同时） the animals had chased（追赶） Jones and his men out onto the road and shut the five-barred（阻挡） gate behind them. And so, almost before they knew it, the uprising was carried through: Jones was driven out, and the farm was theirs. For the first few minutes the animals could hardly believe their good fortune（运气）. Their first act was to gallop（疾驰） right round the boundaries（边界） of the farm, to make sure no human being was hiding on it; then they raced back to the farm buildings to wipe（擦） out the last traces（痕迹） of Jones's hated rule.

[P12] They broke open the harness（马具）-room at the end of the stables. The bits, nose-rings, dog-chains and cruel knives Mr. Jones used to cut pigs and lambs were all thrown down the well. The reins（缰绳）, halters（笼头）, blinkers（眼罩） and nosebags（饲料袋） went on to the fire in the yard. So did the whips. All the animals jumped with joy at the flames. Snowball also threw on the ribbons that decorated the horses' manes and tails on market days. "Ribbons," he said, "should be considered as clothes, which are the mark of a human being.

[P13] All animals should go naked（裸体）." When Boxer heard this, he brought the small straw hat he wore in summer to keep flies out of his ears, and threw it on the fire with the rest, along with everything that reminded them of Mr. Jones. Soon the animals had destroyed everything that reminded them of Mr. Jones. Napoleon then led them back to the store-shed and gave a double ration（配给） of corn to everybody, with two biscuits for each dog. Then they sang 'Animals of England' seven times without stopping, and after that they slept as they had never slept before. But they woke at dawn（黎明） as usual, and suddenly remembering the great thing that had happened, they all raced out into the pasture（牧场） together.

[P14] A little way down the pasture there was a small hill. The animals rushed to the top and looked round in the clear morning light. Yes, it was theirs--everything they could see was theirs! In their joy they jumped round and round and threw themselves into the air. They rolled in the dew（露水）, ate mouthfuls（满口） of sweet summer grass, kicked up lumps（块） of black earth and breathed in its rich smell. Then they walked round the whole farm and looked with silent wonder at the ploughland（耕地）, the hayfield（干草地）, the orchard, the pool, the spinney（小树林）.

[P15] It was as if they had never seen these things before, and even now they could hardly believe it was all theirs. Then they walked back to the farm buildings and stopped in silence outside the farmhouse（农舍） door. That was theirs too, but they were afraid to go in. After a moment, Snowball and Napoleon pushed the door open with their shoulders, and the animals went in one by one, walking very carefully. They walked softly from room to room, afraid to speak above a whisper（低语）, and looked with wonder at the rich and strange things: the beds with soft feather（羽毛） mattresses（床垫）, the looking-glasses, the sofa, the fine carpet, and the picture of Queen Victoria（维多利亚） above the fireplace（壁炉）.

[P16] They were coming down the stairs when they found Mollie was missing. They went back and found her in the best bedroom. She had taken a blue ribbon（丝带） from Mrs. Jones's dressing-table, and was holding it against her shoulder, admiring herself in the glass in a very silly way. The others told her off sharply（尖锐地）, and they went outside. Some hams hanging in the kitchen were taken out for burial（埋葬）, and Boxer's kick stove in the barrel（桶） of beer in the scullery（洗碗间）, but nothing else in the house was touched. They all agreed right there that the farmhouse should be kept as a museum.

[P17] All agreed that no animal must ever live there. They decided this on the spot（地点）. After breakfast, Snowball and Napoleon called them together again. "Comrades（同志们）," said Snowball, "it is half-past six and we have a long day before us. Today we begin the hay harvest. But there is another matter that must be attended to first." The pigs now showed that during the past three months they had taught themselves to read and write from an old spelling book. It had belonged to Mr. Jones's children and had been thrown on the rubbish heap（堆）.

[P18] Napoleon sent for pots of black and white paint and led the way to the five-barred（阻挡） gate on the main road. Snowball (best at writing) took a brush between the knuckles（指关节） of his trotter（猪蹄） and painted out FARM from the top bar（酒吧）, painting ANIMAL FARM instead. This would be the farm's name from then on. Then they went back to the farm buildings. Snowball and Napoleon sent for a ladder and set it against the end wall of the big barn. The pigs, after three months of study, had reduced the principles of Animalism to Seven Commandments（戒律）.

[P19] The Seven Commandments（戒律） would be written on the wall. They would be a law that never changes, and all animals must live by it for ever. A pig could not keep his balance on a ladder easily, but Snowball climbed up and began to work. Squealer stood below him and held the paint-pot. The Commandments were written on the tarred（涂焦油） wall in big white letters. Animals could read them thirty yards away. They were:

THE SEVEN COMMANDMENTS

1. Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy.

2. Whatever goes upon four legs, or has wings, is a friend.

[P20] No animal shall wear clothes. No animal shall sleep in a bed. No animal shall drink alcohol（酒精）. No animal shall kill any other animal. All animals are equal. It was written very neatly（整洁地）. Only "friend" was written "freind（朋友）", and one "S" was the wrong way round. The rest was right. Snowball read it aloud. All the animals nodded, and the cleverer ones began to learn the Commandments by heart. "Now, comrades（同志们）," cried Snowball, throwing down the paint-brush, "to the hayfield! Let us get in the harvest more quickly than Jones and his men could do." But then the three cows, uneasy（不安） for some time, set up a loud lowing.

[P21] They had not been milked for twenty-four hours, and their udders（乳房） were almost bursting（爆裂）. After a little thought, the pigs sent for buckets and milked the cows quite well. Soon there were five buckets of creamy（奶油色） milk, and many animals looked at it with great interest. "What will happen to all that milk?" said someone. "Jones sometimes mixed some of it in our mash（糊状饲料）," said one of the hens. "Never mind the milk, comrades!" cried Napoleon, standing in front of the buckets. "That will be attended to. The harvest is more important. Comrade（同志） Snowball will lead the way.

[P22] I will come soon. Go forward, comrades! The hay is waiting." So the animals went to the hayfield to start the harvest. When they came back, the milk was gone.
